assessment.nobel_worthiness: The heterogeneous-firm trade framework changed how the field thinks about selection, reallocation and the gains from trade. It linked trade theory to firm-level microdata and shaped a large empirical and policy literature. Its influence reaches beyond trade into macroeconomics and productivity.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the central dynamic-selection model, and Helpman's earlier and parallel work on firm heterogeneity, trade in differentiated products and FDI is foundational. Redding is a major later contributor, but the core credit rests most clearly with Melitz and Helpman. Other contributors such as Bernard, Eaton, Kortum and Jensen could be argued for.
assessment.maturity: The Melitz model dates from over 20 years ago, and its predictions and extensions have been extensively tested. The field has had no dedicated prize since 2008, so the timing is mature.
uncertainties: Whether the committee would include Redding or contributors outside this list, such as Bernard, Eaton or Kortum.
Overlap with the quantitative trade candidate (B001) may split support within trade.
The empirical gains-from-trade magnitudes remain debated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Population-scale administrative data opened a new empirical agenda on opportunity, neighborhoods and mobility. The work is highly influential on policy and on how the profession measures inequality of opportunity.
assessment.attribution: Chetty is the central figure, with Hendren and Friedman as long-time collaborators on neighborhood effects and mobility. Katz's Moving to Opportunity work is a related but distinct contribution. Credit is concentrated in a collaborative group, which makes boundaries somewhat fuzzy.
assessment.maturity: The core results are roughly 10 years old, with some replication and follow-up. Long-run policy consequences are still unfolding, and the work is relatively young for a prize.
uncertainties: Whether the contribution is more empirical measurement than conceptual advance.
Overlap with the public economics and inequality candidates (B014, B038).
Timing is early relative to prize norms, and attribution among many co-authors is unclear.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The long-run top-income series reshaped the measurement of inequality and brought distributional evidence into growth and public finance. The work has had large intellectual and policy influence.
assessment.attribution: Piketty and Saez built the top-income series and the long-run evidence, and Zucman extended it to wealth and offshore holdings. Atkinson, now deceased, and other data contributors are important precursors. Credit is clear for the three named, though the theoretical interpretation is more contested.
assessment.maturity: The empirical series are established, but methodological critiques of the distributional accounting and of the theory of r>g remain active. Zucman's contributions are comparatively recent.
uncertainties: Debate over measurement choices and the strength of causal claims.
Whether the committee views the contribution as measurement or as conceptual and theoretical advance.
Recency of Zucman's work relative to the other two.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The New Keynesian framework, built on nominal rigidities, the Taylor rule and the microfounded policy framework, underlies modern central-bank analysis and has had very large practical and academic influence.
assessment.attribution: This is a crowded field. Calvo (pricing), Taylor (staggered contracts and the policy rule) and Woodford (the unifying framework) are the most foundational, but Galí, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets have strong claims. Any three-person selection is therefore contestable.
assessment.maturity: The framework has decades of confirmation and use, so maturity is very high. Some core ideas are older, and critiques and heterogeneity-based revisions are ongoing.
uncertainties: Difficult three-person attribution among at least eight credited names.
Whether the committee favors the original authors or the later synthesis.
The framework's performance after the 2020s inflation episode is debated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The theory of collateral constraints and credit cycles is a foundational mechanism connecting financial frictions to aggregate fluctuations. It has been central in macro-finance research and in understanding financial crises.
assessment.attribution: Kiyotaki and Moore (1997) have a clear and compact joint claim. Gertler and Gilchrist developed the financial accelerator and its empirical side, and Bernanke is a major figure outside the list. Limiting to two keeps the credit sharp.
assessment.maturity: The contribution is about 30 years old and has been widely extended and quantitatively applied, so maturity is high. Empirical identification of the mechanism has been mixed.
uncertainties: Overlap with Bernanke, Gertler and Gilchrist's financial accelerator work, and possible tension with the 2022 prize.
Whether the committee prefers a broader credit-cycle grouping that includes Gertler.
Empirical validation of the amplification mechanism is uneven.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantifying how input misallocation across firms accounts for cross-country TFP differences created a major research program in macro-development. It links micro heterogeneity to aggregate income gaps and has influenced policy thinking on productivity.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh and Klenow (2009) is the core paper, and Restuccia and Rogerson (2008) is a closely parallel and equally foundational contribution. The shortlist of Hsieh, Klenow and Restuccia is defensible, but Rogerson is not credited here. I propose the two with the most influential single paper. Disclosure: Klenow is a long-standing co-author of mine, which I disclose but do not adjudicate.
assessment.maturity: The literature is about 15 to 17 years old and widely replicated, but measurement of the wedges and their interpretation (versus mismeasurement) remains debated.
uncertainties: Measurement error and interpretation of wedges versus true distortions.
Attribution between Hsieh-Klenow and Restuccia-Rogerson.
The author's disclosed co-authorship with Klenow.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The task-based view of technology and the China-shock evidence changed how economists and policymakers understand labor-market polarization, trade exposure and local adjustment. The work is highly influential in both academic and public debate.
assessment.attribution: Autor is the central figure across both strands. Hanson and Dorn are key co-authors on the China shock, while Acemoglu and Restrepo and Autor-Levy-Murnane are relevant for task models. Katz is credited here but more tied to the earlier skill-biased change literature. Attribution is somewhat spread.
assessment.maturity: The China-shock work is about a decade old, and the long-run effects and the lasting local impacts are still being studied. The task framework has been confirmed in many datasets.
uncertainties: Possible overlap with the 2024 growth and institutions prize and with Acemoglu's task-based work.
Persistence and interpretation of China-shock effects.
Attribution between the task framework and the trade-shock empirics.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Structural demand estimation and dynamic industry models made empirical industrial organization quantitative and are widely used in antitrust and regulatory work. The methods have broad application beyond IO.
assessment.attribution: Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes (BLP) are the central names for demand estimation, while Pakes also made foundational contributions to dynamic games (Ericson-Pakes) and production-function estimation. Bresnahan, Reiss and others are also credited here, so the group is large and the attribution is difficult.
assessment.maturity: The methods have been in use for 30 years and are well established, but the contribution is partly methodological and the field has seen competing approaches.
uncertainties: Large credited group and difficult attribution.
Whether the committee views this as a methodological contribution of sufficient breadth.
Sensitivity of results to modeling assumptions.
